_comment: Topic index of DORA24 (Accelerate State of DevOps 2024, v. 2024.3). Page convention: PDF page = printed number (checked: 120 pages; p.1 cover, printed numbers match). Summaries are short paraphrases; the source is the PDF. Portuguese search terms are kept on purpose so Portuguese user input still matches.
source: DORA24 = Accelerate State of DevOps 2024 (Google Cloud / DORA), v. 2024.3, 120 pages, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license (p.118)

entries.summary: Annual research (survey + interviews); key results: AI, user-centricity, transformational leadership, stable priorities, platform, cloud, delivery levels.

Four delivery metrics (lead time, deploy frequency, failure rate, failed deployment recovery time); they measure throughput and stability of code and configuration changes; note 1 (p.16) defines what counts as a failure.
Fifth metric (rework rate) and split into two factors: throughput (lead time, frequency, recovery) and stability (failure rate, rework).
Table of 4 clusters (2024) with values per metric and % of respondents; clusters emerge from the data; figure 1 p.14; elite vs low comparison p.15.
The medium cluster is more stable and less fast than high; there is no universal answer; improving matters more than reaching a level; speed and stability tend to move together (p.79).
Elite versus low: 127x faster lead time, 182x more deploys/year, 8x lower failure rate, 2293x faster recovery (labels checked on the p.15 image).
Industry rarely predicts delivery performance (p.15); reliance on AI is similar across industries (p.19).
Measure per application/service, not per organization; do not compare teams/individuals; do not use as a maturity model; 7-step experimental cycle (p.7); Quick Check and value stream mapping (p.16).
81% of organizations prioritized AI; 75.9% of respondents rely on AI for some task; most common tasks; low trust in 39.2%; future expectations.
For +25% AI adoption: flow +2.6%, satisfaction +2.2%, productivity +2.1%; time on valuable work -2.6%; toil and burnout with no clear effect; vacuum hypothesis.
For +25% AI: documentation +7.5%, code quality +3.4%, review speed +3.1%, approval +1.3%, complexity -1.8%; technical debt and coordination ~0 (intervals cross zero).
For +25% AI: delivery throughput -1.5% and stability -7.2% (estimates); hypothesis: larger batches; improving the process does not automatically improve delivery.
For +25% AI: organization +2.3%, team +1.4%, product ~+0.2% with no obvious association; product-team correlation r=0.56 and product-organization r=0.47; figure 12 is an abstraction, not data.
Three recommendations: clear mission/policies, culture of learning and experimentation (including test automation), acknowledge trade-offs and measure downstream impacts.
Platform as a sociotechnical discipline; golden paths = automated self-service flows; user-centered approach (developers).
IDP users: individual productivity +8%, team +10%, organization +6%; 89% use an IDP (broad definition); developer independence +5%; dedicated team +6% only at team level; J-curve by age.

Throughput -8% and stability -14% with a platform; exclusive use -6% throughput; instability + platform linked to burnout (uncertain cause); three hypotheses; mitigations (feedback, SLO/error budget, escape hatches from the automations).

User focus increases productivity and satisfaction and reduces burnout; with high focus, product quality does not depend on fast/stable delivery; with low focus, delivery is the only path (fig.15 p.60).
Quality documentation amplifies the effect of user focus on product performance (fig.16); without user signals, the effect is not significant; documentation culture practices.

Unstable priorities: small drop in productivity and substantial increase in burnout, not mitigated by leadership, docs or user focus; stabilizing priorities reduces delivery speed/stability (intriguing finding); AI in products stabilizes priorities but -10% delivery stability.

Five dimensions; +25% transformational leadership: productivity ~+9% (p.71 text; 8.7% in fig.18), burnout -9.9%, satisfaction +9.1%, team +8.7%, product +4.5%, organization +10.3%; it is enabling, not sufficient.

More than 30 capabilities/processes (list on the dora.dev site, not in the report); four keys per application/service; combine technical and business metrics; user feedback metrics as important as the four keys.
Using cloud without the 5 NIST characteristics may predict lower organizational performance (2023 finding, reiterated); iterate starting with a few services.
Initial drop followed by gains (DevOps, SRE, platform); transformation is a journey, not a destination.
2009-2024 timeline: Flickr/DevOpsDays, Puppet reports, Forsgren 2014, DORA 2016, Accelerate book 2017, Google Cloud acquisition 2018.
High-trust culture is one of the best performance predictors; the biggest predictor of application development security practices (2022 research); Westrum cited as inspiration.

Operational performance (studied since 2018) measures keeping promises about the product; best results when delivery and operations go together; SLOs/error budgets suggested to calibrate appetite for instability (p.55). No detailed operational metrics.
About 3,000 respondents in 2024 (39,000 over the decade); 104 countries; 35.69% technology; 83% men; median 16 years of experience; compared with Stack Overflow 2023 without major discrepancies.
Question selection; localization into 6 languages; organic (snowball) recruitment + panel; three random flows (AI, work environment, platform); 11 interviews.
Measure validation (CFA/lavaan), model comparison (LOOCV, WAIC), Bayesian statistics, 89% intervals, posterior simulations.
No longitudinal study or experiment; temporal precedence is theoretical; biases handled via DAGs (theoretical); micro->macro leap assumed by probabilistic heuristic.
Many small models instead of one giant; default question 'if we do X, what happens to Y'; schematic model repeated per capability; effects vary by capability.
Treat findings as hypotheses; replicate, run internal experiments and surveys, share what you learn.
List of readings and links (Team Topologies, Accelerate, Quick Check, capabilities, trust in AI).

gaps.hint: The report uses 'failed deployment recovery time' (p.10); it does not use the MTTR acronym nor 'time to restore' (grep on the text: 0 occurrences). Names from earlier editions are [DATED]/outside the collection.
The report uses 'change lead time' (p.10), not 'lead time for changes'.
Technical capabilities (CI/CD, trunk-based etc.) are only pointed to dora.dev/capabilities (p.16; p.56 notes); not detailed in the report.
Specific technologies are not covered in the report (0 occurrences).
Other productivity/DevEx frameworks are not covered (0 occurrences of DevEx and cognitive load).
Supply chain security is not covered; there is only one mention of culture as a predictor of security practices (p.81, 2022 research).
Observability is practically not covered (one tangential mention; no content).
Safe deployment techniques are not covered; 'rollbacks' appears only in the failure rate definition (p.10).
The report cites the ROI of DevOps whitepaper (2020) but does not include the formulas (p.72, p.78).
The PDF is from 2024 (v. 2024.3). Later editions are not in the collection; mark [DATED] and check dora.dev.
The report advises against comparing teams and individuals with the four keys (p.74).
